stem: Water is an amphoteric compound that also acts as a good solvent of polar and ionic compounds.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.stem:
Equation 1 shows water acting as a Brønsted-Lowry acid.

equation 1 $$\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NO}_2^- \rightleftharpoons \text{HNO}_2 + \text{OH}^-$$
parts.text:
Identify the **two** conjugate acid-base pairs in equation 1.

{{figure:pdf_visual_01.png}}

acid I $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ conjugate base of acid I

acid II conjugate base of acid II

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
Water also behaves as a Brønsted-Lowry acid when it dissolves $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$.

Explain the ability of $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ to act as a base.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Write an equation to show water acting as a base with $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem:
The ionic product of water, $K_\text{w}$, measures the extent to which water dissociates.

$$\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$$

Fig. 2.1 shows how $K_\text{w}$ varies with temperature.

{{figure:pdf_visual_02.png}}

Fig. 2.1

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Use information from Fig. 2.1 to deduce whether the dissociation of water is an exothermic or an endothermic process.

Explain your answer.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
An aqueous solution has $\text{pH} = 7.00$ at $30^\circ\text{C}$.

Use information from Fig. 2.1 to explain why this solution can be considered to be alkaline at $30^\circ\text{C}$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.stem:
The three physical states of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ have different standard entropies, $S^\ominus$, associated with them. Table 2.1 shows these $S^\ominus$ values.

Table 2.1

| state of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ | standard entropy, $S^\ominus / \text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| solid | +48.0 |
| liquid | +70.1 |
| gas | +188.7 |
parts.text: Explain the difference in the $S^\ominus$ values of $\text{H}_2\text{O(s)}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why the increase in $S^\ominus$ is **much** greater when $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ boils than when it melts.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text:
The energy changes for $\text{H}_2\text{O(s)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ are shown.

$$\Delta G = 0.00 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$\Delta H = +6.03 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Use these data to show that the melting point of $\text{H}_2\text{O(s)}$ is $0^\circ\text{C}$.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.stem:
Metal-air batteries are electrochemical cells that generate electrical energy from the reaction of metal anodes with air.

The standard electrode potentials for the zinc-air battery are shown.

$$[\text{Zn(OH)}_4]^{2-} + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Zn} + 4\text{OH}^- \qquad E^\ominus = -1.22\text{ V}$$
$$\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{OH}^- \qquad E^\ominus = +0.40\text{ V}$$
parts.text: Calculate the standard cell potential, $E^\ominus_\text{cell}$, of the zinc-air battery.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text:
The zinc-air battery usually operates at pH11 and 298K. The overall cell potential is dependent on $[\text{OH}^-]$.

The Nernst equation shows how the electrode potential at the cathode changes with $[\text{OH}^-]$.

$$E = 0.40 - (\frac{0.059}{z}) \log([\text{OH}^-]^2)$$

Calculate the electrode potential, $E$, at pH11.
